h: Koalas have fingerprints a lot like ours.
t: Under a microscope, koala fingerprints look so similar to human prints that even experts can struggle to tell them apart. The ridges probably help koalas grip branches and feel the leaves they eat.

h: Wombats make cube-shaped poop.
t: The walls of a wombat's intestine stretch unevenly, slowly shaping its droppings into little cubes. Wombats leave them on rocks and logs to mark their territory, and the flat sides stop them from rolling away.

h: A giraffe's neck has just seven bones.
t: That's the same number of neck bones that humans have. Each giraffe vertebra is simply enormous, and a single one can be about 25 centimeters long.

h: Polar bears have black skin.
t: Their fur isn't truly white either: each hair is see-through and only looks white because it scatters light, the same way snow does. The dark skin underneath helps soak up warmth.

h: Platypuses lay eggs.
t: The platypus and the echidnas are the only mammals that lay eggs instead of giving birth to live young. A platypus can also sense the tiny electrical signals made by its prey, using its rubbery bill.

h: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
t: Flying squirrels can only glide, but bats flap their way through the air. A bat's wing is really a hand, with long finger bones covered by a thin layer of skin.

h: A cow has one stomach with four compartments.
t: People often say cows have four stomachs, but it's really one stomach divided into four chambers. Together they let a cow break down tough grass that most animals can't digest.

h: A rodent's front teeth never stop growing.
t: Squirrels, mice and beavers must keep gnawing to wear their front teeth down. Beaver teeth even look orange because their enamel contains iron, which makes it extra tough.

h: Cheetahs can't roar, but they can purr.
t: Instead of roaring like lions, cheetahs purr, chirp and make bird-like yelps to talk to each other.

h: Hippos make their own sunscreen.
t: Hippos ooze a reddish-orange liquid often nicknamed "blood sweat," even though it's neither blood nor sweat. Scientists found that it helps block sunlight and may protect against germs.

h: Hummingbirds can fly backward.
t: By twisting their wings in a figure-eight motion, hummingbirds can hover in place, zip sideways and even reverse away from a flower.

h: An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.
t: Each eye is about five centimeters across, giving ostriches excellent eyesight for spotting danger across open plains.

h: Owls can't move their eyes.
t: An owl's eyes are shaped more like tubes than balls, so they're locked in place. To look around, owls turn their super-flexible necks, up to about 270 degrees.

h: Flamingos are pink because of what they eat.
t: The algae and tiny shrimp in their diet contain natural pigments called carotenoids. A flamingo that eats less of that food slowly turns paler.

h: Some birds sleep with half their brain awake.
t: Ducks resting at the edge of a group can keep one eye open and one side of the brain alert, watching for predators while the other side rests.

h: Crows can remember human faces.
t: In studies, crows recognized people who had bothered them and scolded them years later. They even taught other crows to scold the same people.

h: A woodpecker's tongue wraps around its skull.
t: The tongue is anchored by long, flexible bones that curl around the back of the head, letting woodpeckers reach deep into holes to grab insects.

h: Arctic terns enjoy two summers every year.
t: These seabirds fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back again each year, a round trip of tens of thousands of kilometers.

h: Peregrine falcons are among the fastest animals on Earth.
t: In a hunting dive called a stoop, a peregrine can reach speeds of more than 300 km/h.

h: Lyrebirds can copy almost any sound.
t: These Australian birds weave other birds' songs into their own, and some have been recorded imitating camera clicks and car alarms.

h: Butterflies taste with their feet.
t: Sensors on their feet tell a butterfly whether a leaf is the right plant for its eggs, just by standing on it.

h: Honeybees dance to give directions.
t: A bee returning to the hive performs a "waggle dance" whose angle and length tell other bees which way to fly and how far to go to find flowers.

h: Bees have five eyes.
t: Two big compound eyes see shapes and movement, while three tiny eyes on top of the head help sense light.

h: Insects don't have lungs.
t: They breathe through tiny holes along their bodies called spiracles, which lead into a network of air tubes.

h: Spider silk can be stronger than steel of the same weight.
t: Some silks are stretchy too, which lets a web catch fast-flying insects without snapping.

h: Fireflies make "cold" light.
t: The chemical reaction that makes a firefly glow gives off very little heat, unlike an old-fashioned light bulb. Many species flash in their own special pattern to find a mate.

h: Dragonflies have up to about 30,000 lenses in each eye.
t: Their huge eyes give them nearly all-around vision, and they can fly forward, backward, sideways or hover in place.

h: A cricket's ears are on its front legs.
t: Tiny drum-like patches just below the knees pick up the chirps of other crickets.

h: Monarch butterfly migration takes several generations.
t: Monarchs from eastern North America fly thousands of kilometers to spend the winter in Mexico, and no single butterfly makes the whole round trip.

h: Only female mosquitoes bite.
t: Both males and females sip plant nectar, but females need a meal of blood to make their eggs.

h: Wood frogs can freeze solid and survive.
t: In winter, a wood frog's heart stops and ice forms inside its body, while special sugars protect its cells. When spring arrives, it thaws out and hops away.

h: Chameleons change color mostly to communicate.
t: Tiny crystals in their skin reflect light differently as they shift. Color changes signal mood, warn rivals and help control body temperature, not just help them hide.

h: A turtle can't climb out of its shell.
t: The shell is part of its skeleton, built from the turtle's own ribs and backbone fused together.

h: Nest temperature decides whether many baby turtles are boys or girls.
t: In many turtle species, warmer nests produce more females and cooler nests produce more males.

h: Snakes smell with their tongues.
t: A flicking tongue collects scent particles from the air and delivers them to a special sensing organ in the roof of the mouth.

h: Geckos can walk across ceilings.
t: Their toes are covered in millions of microscopic hairs that cling to surfaces using tiny attractive forces between molecules.

h: Axolotls can regrow lost body parts.
t: These Mexican salamanders can rebuild legs, tails and even parts of their heart and spinal cord.

h: Some lizards can drop their tails to escape.
t: The wriggling tail distracts a predator while the lizard dashes away, and many species slowly grow a new one.

h: Pit vipers can sense heat.
t: Small pits on their faces detect infrared warmth, so they can find warm-blooded animals even in total darkness.

h: Glass frogs have see-through bellies.
t: Look at one from underneath and you can watch its heart beating inside.

h: Mantis shrimp pack one of the fastest punches in nature.
t: Their club-like limbs strike quickly enough to crack snail shells, and their eyes have far more types of color receptors than ours.

h: Elephants can feel rumbles through their feet.
t: Elephants make deep, low calls that travel through the ground, and they can pick up those vibrations with their sensitive feet and trunks.

h: The star-nosed mole has an amazing nose.
t: The 22 pink tentacles around its snout are packed with touch sensors, helping it find and gobble food in a fraction of a second.

h: Sharks can sense electricity.
t: Jelly-filled pores on a shark's snout detect the faint electrical signals made by the muscles of other animals.

h: A dog's nose print is one of a kind.
t: Just like human fingerprints, the pattern of ridges and bumps on a dog's nose is different for every dog.

h: Cats can't taste sweetness.
t: Cats lack a working version of the gene for detecting sweet flavors, which makes sense for animals that mostly eat meat.

h: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
t: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one pumps it around the body. Their blood uses copper instead of iron to carry oxygen, which gives it a blue tint.

h: Camel humps store fat, not water.
t: The fat is an energy reserve. Camels survive long dry spells because their bodies are extremely good at saving water.

h: Snow leopards use their tails as scarves.
t: Their long, fluffy tails help them balance on steep slopes and can be wrapped around their faces to keep warm.

h: Tardigrades can survive a trip to space.
t: These tiny "water bears" can dry out into a tough little ball and survive freezing cold, crushing pressure and even exposure to outer space.

h: Seahorse dads give birth.
t: The female places her eggs in a pouch on the male's belly, and he carries them until the tiny babies swim out.

h: Emperor penguin fathers balance the egg on their feet.
t: For about two months of freezing Antarctic winter, the dad keeps the egg warm under a feathery fold of skin while the mom goes to sea to feed.

h: A newborn kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean.
t: The tiny joey is born after only about a month, then crawls into its mother's pouch, where it keeps growing for months.

h: Sea otters sometimes hold paws while they nap.
t: Floating otters may link paws or wrap themselves in kelp so they don't drift away from their group.

h: Bottlenose dolphins have names.
t: Each dolphin develops its own "signature whistle," and other dolphins can copy that whistle to call a specific friend.

h: Elephant families are led by the oldest female.
t: A herd is usually guided by an experienced matriarch, whose memory of water holes and safe routes helps the whole family.

h: Meerkats take turns standing guard.
t: While the group digs for food, one meerkat keeps watch from a high spot and gives an alarm call if danger appears.

h: Leafcutter ants are farmers.
t: They don't eat the leaves they carry. Instead they use them to grow a special fungus in underground gardens, and the fungus becomes their food.

h: Termite mounds are built to breathe.
t: Tunnels and chimneys inside the mound help air flow through it, and architects have studied them while designing buildings that stay cool with less energy.

h: Animal groups have wonderful names.
t: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance, and a group of owls is called a parliament.

h: Bananas are berries, but strawberries aren't.
t: To a botanist, a berry is a fleshy fruit that grows from a single flower with one ovary and usually holds its seeds inside. Bananas fit that description, while strawberries don't.

h: A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside.
t: Each little speck on the surface is actually a tiny fruit with a seed inside it. The sweet red part is the swollen tip of the flower stem.

h: Tomatoes once went all the way to the Supreme Court.
t: In 1893, the US Supreme Court ruled that tomatoes should be taxed as vegetables because people cook and serve them like vegetables, even though botanists call them fruits.

h: A pineapple is lots of fruits fused together.
t: Each bumpy segment on its skin grew from its own flower, and the segments merge into one big fruit as it develops.

h: Avocados are giant berries.
t: Botanically, an avocado is a berry with one large seed. Its bumpy green skin once earned it the nickname "alligator pear."

h: Every bump on a raspberry is a mini fruit.
t: A raspberry is a cluster of tiny fruits called drupelets, and each one holds its own seed. That's why raspberries feel a little crunchy.

h: Apples float because they're partly air.
t: Roughly a quarter of a fresh apple's volume is air tucked between its cells, which is what makes bobbing for apples possible.

h: Apples, cherries and peaches belong to the rose family.
t: Pears, plums, apricots, almonds and raspberries are relatives too. They all share the same big plant family as the roses in a garden.

h: Broccoli, cabbage, kale and cauliflower are the same species.
t: Over centuries, farmers bred one wild cabbage plant in different directions, favouring big leaves, tight heads or chunky flower clusters. Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi came from that same plant.

h: Broccoli is a bunch of flowers.
t: Its florets are clusters of unopened flower buds. Artichokes are flower buds too, from a kind of thistle.

h: Peanuts aren't nuts.
t: They're legumes, in the same family as peas and beans. After a peanut flower is pollinated, its stalk bends down and pushes into the soil, where the pod grows underground.

h: Cashews hang from the bottom of a fruit.
t: Each one grows beneath a juicy, bell-shaped fruit called a cashew apple. The shell holds an oil that irritates skin, which is why cashews are always sold already shelled.

h: Sweet potatoes aren't close cousins of potatoes.
t: Sweet potatoes belong to the morning glory family, while regular potatoes are related to tomatoes, peppers and eggplants.

h: Green bell peppers are simply picked early.
t: Left on the plant longer, many varieties ripen to red, yellow or orange and taste sweeter.

h: Every strand of corn silk leads to a single kernel.
t: Each silk has to catch a grain of pollen for its kernel to grow, which is why a poorly pollinated cob ends up with gaps.

h: Carrots weren't always orange.
t: Many early cultivated carrots were purple or yellow. The orange carrots we know today became popular in Europe only a few hundred years ago.

h: Popcorn pops thanks to a tiny steam explosion.
t: Each kernel holds a little water. As it heats, the water turns to steam, pressure builds inside the tough hull, and the kernel bursts and turns inside out.

h: Onions make you cry to protect themselves.
t: Slicing an onion breaks its cells and releases a chemical that floats up as a gas and stings your eyes. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction down.

h: Cut apples turn brown because of oxygen.
t: Once the flesh is exposed, natural enzymes react with oxygen in the air. A squeeze of lemon juice slows the browning because the acid gets in the way.

h: Bananas help other fruit ripen.
t: Ripening bananas give off a natural gas called ethylene. Put an unripe pear or avocado in a paper bag with a banana and it will soften sooner.

h: Water boils at a lower temperature on mountaintops.
t: With less air pressure pushing down, water boils before it reaches 100°C, so pasta and boiled eggs take longer to cook at high altitude.

h: Toast browns because of a chemical reaction.
t: Heat makes sugars and proteins react in a process called the Maillard reaction, which creates new flavors and aromas. The same reaction browns cookies, roasted vegetables and grilled cheese.

h: A spin can tell you whether an egg is cooked.
t: A hard-boiled egg spins smoothly, while a raw egg wobbles because its liquid insides slosh around. Stop a spinning raw egg for a moment, let go, and it may start turning again.

h: Old eggs float.
t: An eggshell is covered in thousands of tiny pores. Over time, moisture escapes and air seeps in, so the air pocket inside grows until the egg is light enough to float.

h: Much of what you call taste is really smell.
t: Your tongue senses a handful of basic tastes, but your nose picks up a huge range of aromas. Pinch your nose while eating a jellybean and most of the flavor vanishes.

h: Umami got its name in 1908.
t: Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda studied the savoury taste of seaweed broth and named it umami. Today it's counted as one of the five basic tastes, along with sweet, salty, sour and bitter.

h: Mint feels cold, but it isn't.
t: A compound in mint called menthol switches on the same nerve sensors that detect cold, so your mouth feels cool even though its temperature hasn't changed.

h: Chili heat isn't a taste.
t: The burn comes from capsaicin, which sets off pain and heat sensors rather than taste buds. Birds don't feel it, so they happily eat wild chili peppers and spread the seeds.

h: Chocolate melts just below body temperature.
t: Cocoa butter turns liquid at a temperature a little cooler than the inside of your mouth, which is why a square of chocolate stays firm in the wrapper but goes smooth on your tongue.

h: White chocolate contains no cocoa solids.
t: It's made from cocoa butter, sugar and milk, which is why it has none of the dark color or bitterness of other chocolate.

h: Your taste cells are always being replaced.
t: The cells in your taste buds wear out and are replaced roughly every couple of weeks, so your sense of taste is constantly renewing itself.

h: Tomatoes didn't reach Italy until the 1500s.
t: Tomatoes, potatoes, corn, chili peppers and cacao all came from the Americas and only spread to Europe, Africa and Asia after 1492. Before then, Italian cooking had no tomato sauce at all.

h: Chocolate started out as a bitter drink.
t: The Maya and Aztecs ground cacao beans into frothy, unsweetened drinks, often spiced with chili. Cacao beans were so valued that people used them like money.

h: Ketchup didn't always contain tomatoes.
t: The name probably comes from a fermented fish sauce from southern China, and early European versions were made with mushrooms, walnuts or oysters. Tomato ketchup came along later.

h: Pepper was once valuable enough to pay the rent.
t: In medieval Europe, peppercorns were sometimes accepted for rents and taxes. In English, a "peppercorn rent" still means a tiny, symbolic payment.

h: People were chewing gum thousands of years ago.
t: Ancient people in Scandinavia chewed lumps of birch bark tar, and the Maya chewed chicle, a natural gum from the sapodilla tree.

h: A dentist helped invent cotton candy.
t: In the 1890s, dentist William Morrison and candy maker John C. Wharton built a machine that spun melted sugar into fluffy threads. They sold it to huge crowds at the 1904 World's Fair, calling it fairy floss.

h: Caesar salad isn't named after Julius Caesar.
t: It's usually credited to Caesar Cardini, an Italian-born restaurant owner who served it in Tijuana, Mexico, in the 1920s.

h: Vanilla comes from an orchid.
t: The flavor comes from the cured seed pods of a climbing orchid. On many farms, each flower is still pollinated by hand, using a method worked out in 1841 by a 12-year-old boy named Edmond Albius on the island of Réunion.

h: Saffron threads are parts of a flower.
t: Each thread is a stigma from a crocus flower, picked by hand. It takes a huge number of blossoms to make a small amount, which is why saffron is so pricey.

h: Nutmeg and mace come from the same fruit.
t: Nutmeg is the seed, and mace is the lacy red covering wrapped around it.

h: Honey almost never spoils.
t: It's very low in water and slightly acidic, which makes it a terrible home for germs. Archaeologists have even found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs.

h: Cranberries bounce and float.
t: Ripe cranberries have little pockets of air inside. Many growers flood their fields at harvest time so the berries rise to the surface and can be gathered up.

h: Planting an apple seed won't grow the same apple.
t: A tree grown from a seed produces fruit that's different from its parent's. To keep a favorite variety, growers attach cuttings to other trees in a process called grafting.

h: Supermarket bananas are clones.
t: Common store bananas don't have working seeds, so new plants are grown from shoots of existing ones. That makes them genetically almost identical to each other.

h: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
t: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC, about 2,500 years before Cleopatra was born. Only about 2,000 years separate her life from the first Moon landing in 1969.

h: Cleopatra was the first in her royal family to speak Egyptian.
t: Her family was of Greek descent and had ruled Egypt for about 250 years. Ancient writers say she was the first of them to bother learning the language of the people she ruled.

h: Ancient Egyptians loved board games.
t: One favorite, called senet, was played on a long board of 30 squares. It was so cherished that sets were placed in tombs, including several in the tomb of the young pharaoh Tutankhamun.

h: Egyptians often slept on headrests instead of soft pillows.
t: These curved stands of wood, stone or ivory cradled the neck and held the head off the bed, and they were probably padded with cloth for comfort.

h: Ancient Romans grabbed fast food from street counters.
t: Many city dwellers lived in small apartments without kitchens, so they bought hot meals at counters called thermopolia. Archaeologists have uncovered dozens of them in the ruins of Pompeii.

h: The word plumbing comes from the Latin word for lead.
t: Romans called lead plumbum and often used it to make water pipes. That's also why lead's chemical symbol is Pb.

h: Some of the oldest known musical instruments are flutes made of bone.
t: Flutes carved from bird bones and mammoth ivory, found in caves in Germany, are more than 35,000 years old. People were making music long before they were writing.

h: Teenagers discovered the famous cave paintings at Lascaux.
t: In 1940, four teenagers in southwestern France squeezed into a hole and found cave walls covered in painted horses, deer and bulls. The artwork is roughly 17,000 years old.

h: The first ice skates were made from animal bones.
t: Thousands of years ago, people in northern Europe tied flattened bones to their feet so they could glide across frozen lakes instead of walking around them.

h: One of the oldest leather shoes ever found is about 5,500 years old.
t: Discovered in a cave in Armenia, it was made from a single piece of cowhide, laced up the front and stuffed with grass, possibly to keep its shape.

h: A man who lived over 5,000 years ago was found in the Alps in 1991.
t: Nicknamed Ötzi, he was preserved so well by ice that scientists could study his clothes, his tools and even dozens of small tattoos on his skin.

h: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid was built.
t: A small group survived on Wrangel Island, off the coast of Siberia, until about 4,000 years ago, centuries after the pyramid was finished.

h: Some of the earliest writing was bookkeeping.
t: Many of the oldest clay tablets from ancient Mesopotamia, more than 5,000 years old, are records of grain, livestock and goods. Writing may have started as a way to keep track of who owned what.

h: The Rosetta Stone cracked the code of hieroglyphs.
t: Found in Egypt in 1799, it repeats the same message in hieroglyphs, another Egyptian script and ancient Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek, Jean-François Champollion was able to decode the hieroglyphs in 1822.

h: We count minutes and seconds in sixties because of ancient Mesopotamia.
t: Mathematicians there used a number system based on 60. That legacy lives on in 60-minute hours and 360-degree circles.

h: Rome's Pantheon has a hole in its roof on purpose.
t: The round opening at the top of its concrete dome, called the oculus, is the building's main source of light. When it rains, water falls inside and drains away through holes in the floor. The dome has stood for about 1,900 years.

h: There was a vending machine in the first century.
t: Hero of Alexandria, a Greek engineer, described a device that released a small amount of water when someone dropped a coin into a slot. The coin's weight tipped a lever that opened a valve.

h: The ancient Greeks built a gear-driven calculator.
t: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from an ancient shipwreck in the early 1900s, is more than 2,000 years old. Its bronze gears could predict eclipses and track the movements of the Sun and Moon.

h: Papermaking was perfected in ancient China.
t: A court official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving the process around the year 105, using materials such as tree bark, old rags and hemp.

h: Movable type was invented in China centuries before it reached Europe.
t: Around the 1040s, an inventor named Bi Sheng made individual characters from baked clay that could be arranged, printed and reused, roughly 400 years before Gutenberg's printing press.

h: Paper money began in China.
t: About 1,000 years ago, merchants and then the government in China started using printed paper notes, because carrying heavy strings of metal coins was such a hassle.

h: Kites have been flying for more than 2,000 years.
t: They were invented in ancient China, where early kites were made of silk or paper stretched over bamboo frames.

h: Chess began in India.
t: The game traces back to one played in India around 1,500 years ago. It spread to Persia and then Europe, and its pieces and rules changed along the way.

h: Eyeglasses were invented in Italy in the late 1200s.
t: The first pairs had no arms to rest on the ears. People balanced them on their noses or held them in front of their eyes.

h: Bristle toothbrushes came from China.
t: By the late 1400s, people in China were brushing with stiff hog bristles attached to handles made of bone or bamboo.

h: People once erased pencil marks with bread.
t: In 1770, scientist Joseph Priestley wrote about a gummy substance from rubber trees that was excellent for rubbing out pencil marks. That's why many people still call an eraser a "rubber."

h: The first stethoscope was a rolled-up sheet of paper.
t: In 1816, French doctor René Laennec felt awkward pressing his ear to a patient's chest, so he rolled up some paper and listened through the tube. The heartbeat sounded clearer than ever, and he went on to design a wooden version.

h: Braille was created by a teenager.
t: Louis Braille, who was blind from early childhood, had worked out his system of raised dots by about age 15. It's still used around the world for reading by touch.

h: The first hot-air balloon passengers were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
t: In 1783, the French brothers Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier sent the three animals aloft near Versailles to make sure flying was safe. They landed unharmed, and human passengers took to the sky a couple of months later.

h: A melted candy bar led to the microwave oven.
t: In the 1940s, engineer Percy Spencer was working near radar equipment when he noticed that a candy bar in his pocket had melted. He experimented further, starting with popcorn kernels, and helped create the first microwave oven.

h: Penicillin was discovered thanks to a messy lab.
t: In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find mold growing in one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mold, the bacteria had disappeared, and that mold gave the world one of its first antibiotics.

h: A walk in the woods inspired hook-and-loop fasteners.
t: In 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed burrs clinging to his clothes and his dog's fur. Under a microscope he saw tiny hooks grabbing onto loops, and he spent years copying the idea in fabric.

h: The first photograph took hours to make.
t: Around 1826, French inventor Nicéphore Niépce captured the view from his window on a coated metal plate. It needed an exposure lasting many hours, so only things that stayed perfectly still showed up.

h: The first powered airplane flight lasted just 12 seconds.
t: On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright flew about 37 meters at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. That's a shorter distance than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.

h: Ada Lovelace wrote a computer program before computers existed.
t: In 1843, she published notes on Charles Babbage's design for a mechanical computer, including step-by-step instructions for calculating a series of numbers. She's often called the first computer programmer.

h: Alexander Graham Bell wanted people to answer the phone with "ahoy."
t: Thomas Edison favoured "hello," and Edison's choice is the one that caught on.

h: The first computer bug was a real bug.
t: In 1947, operators of an early computer at Harvard found a moth stuck in one of its parts. They taped it into their logbook as a joke, since engineers already used the word "bug" for a glitch.

h: One of the first webcams watched a coffee pot.
t: In 1991, computer scientists at the University of Cambridge pointed a camera at the coffee pot down the hall so they could see whether it was full before making the trip. It was later put online for the whole world to watch.

h: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.
t: Teaching was happening at Oxford by 1096, while the Aztec capital city of Tenochtitlan wasn't founded until 1325.

h: Some countries skipped whole days when they changed calendars.
t: When parts of Europe switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1582, October 4 was followed directly by October 15. Britain and its colonies made the switch in 1752 and skipped 11 days.

h: Before alarm clocks were common, people paid knocker-uppers.
t: In Britain and Ireland, these early risers walked the streets tapping on bedroom windows with long poles, or even firing dried peas with peashooters, to wake workers in time for their shifts.

h: A few children were once sent by mail.
t: After the US began its parcel post service in 1913, a handful of families mailed young children to relatives because postage was cheaper than a train ticket. Postal officials soon put a stop to it.

h: The Eiffel Tower was supposed to be temporary.
t: It was built for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris with a permit to stand for 20 years. Its usefulness as a giant radio antenna helped save it.

h: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown.
t: It's covered in copper, which was shiny and reddish-brown when the statue was unveiled in 1886. Over the following decades, air and weather slowly coated it in the green layer we see today.

h: Vikings reached North America about 500 years before Columbus.
t: Archaeologists have found the remains of a Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada, dating to roughly 1,000 years ago.

h: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in our solar system.
t: All the planets, moons, asteroids and comets put together make up only a tiny leftover sliver.

h: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
t: When you see the Sun, you're seeing it as it looked roughly eight minutes earlier.

h: About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
t: Even so, the Sun is only a medium-sized star compared with some of the giants out there.

h: The Sun is actually white.
t: It gives off every color of visible light, which mixes together into white. Earth's air scatters some blue light away, which is why it looks yellowish from the ground.

h: The center of the Sun is about 15 million °C.
t: At that heat and pressure, hydrogen atoms smash together to make helium, releasing the energy that lights and warms our planet.

h: Northern and southern lights start at the Sun.
t: Streams of charged particles from the Sun hit gases high in Earth's atmosphere and make them glow. Oxygen gives off the familiar green color.

h: The Sun is about halfway through its life.
t: It formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago, and scientists expect it to keep shining steadily for around another 5 billion years.

h: A day on Venus is longer than its year.
t: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 Earth days to travel around the Sun.

h: On Venus, the Sun rises in the west.
t: Venus spins in the opposite direction from most planets, so its sunrise and sunset are flipped compared with ours.

h: Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
t: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat like a heavy blanket, making the surface hot enough to melt lead.

h: Mercury swings between scorching and freezing.
t: With almost no atmosphere to hold heat, its daytime side can reach about 430 °C while its night side plunges to around −180 °C.

h: Mars is red because it's rusty.
t: Its soil and dust contain lots of iron oxide, the same stuff that makes old bikes turn orange-brown.

h: Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system.
t: Olympus Mons rises more than twice as high as Mount Everest, and its base is about 600 kilometers across.

h: Sunsets on Mars look blue.
t: Fine Martian dust scatters light in a way that makes a blue glow around the setting Sun, the opposite of the reddish sunsets we see on Earth.

h: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.
t: It's so big that all the other planets could fit inside it.

h: Jupiter has the shortest day of any planet.
t: This giant spins once in just under 10 hours, which makes it bulge out noticeably at its middle.

h: Saturn is less dense than water.
t: If you could somehow find a bathtub big enough, the gas giant would float.

h: Saturn's rings are mostly ice.
t: The pieces range from specks smaller than sand grains to chunks as big as houses, and the main rings are amazingly thin, in many places only about 10 meters thick.

h: Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side.
t: Its axis is tipped over by about 98 degrees, possibly because something huge knocked into it long ago.

h: Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system.
t: Its winds can whip around the planet at about 2,000 km/h, even though it is very far from the Sun's warmth.

h: Neptune was found with maths before anyone saw it.
t: In 1846, astronomers noticed Uranus wobbling in its path, calculated where an unseen planet should be, and found Neptune right near the predicted spot.

h: The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth.
t: Laser measurements show it moves about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

h: We always see the same side of the Moon.
t: The Moon spins exactly once for every trip around Earth, so the same face always points toward us.

h: Astronaut footprints on the Moon could last for millions of years.
t: With no wind or rain to wipe them away, the bootprints left by Apollo astronauts should stay put for an extremely long time.

h: The Moon has moonquakes.
t: Instruments left behind by Apollo astronauts recorded the Moon's surface shaking, sometimes for many minutes at a time.

h: Total solar eclipses are a cosmic coincidence.
t: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost exactly the same size in our sky.

h: The sky on the Moon is black, even in daytime.
t: Earth's sky is blue because air scatters sunlight. The Moon has almost no air, so its sky stays dark while the Sun shines.

h: The Moon was probably born from a giant crash.
t: The leading idea is that a Mars-sized object slammed into the young Earth, and the debris thrown into space clumped together to form the Moon.

h: Looking at the stars is looking back in time.
t: Starlight can take years, centuries or even longer to reach us, so you're seeing each star as it was when that light set off.

h: The nearest star after the Sun is about 4.2 light-years away.
t: Its name is Proxima Centauri, and its light takes more than four years to reach Earth.

h: A sugar cube of neutron star would weigh about a billion metric tons.
t: Neutron stars are the squashed cores of exploded stars, packing more mass than the Sun into a ball about the size of a city.

h: A star's color reveals its temperature.
t: Blue-white stars are the hottest and reddish stars are the coolest. Our Sun sits in between.

h: Stars twinkle because of Earth's air.
t: Moving pockets of air bend starlight back and forth. Planets usually shine more steadily because they appear as tiny discs instead of single points.

h: The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars.
t: Our Sun is just one of them, sitting in one of the galaxy's spiral arms.

h: The solar system takes about 230 million years to circle the galaxy.
t: The last time Earth was in this part of its galactic orbit, the earliest dinosaurs were just appearing.

h: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away.
t: Under dark skies it looks like a faint, fuzzy smudge, making it one of the most distant things you can see without a telescope.

h: A giant black hole sits at the heart of our galaxy.
t: Called Sagittarius A*, it has about four million times the mass of the Sun, and astronomers released the first image of it in 2022.

h: You are made of star stuff.
t: Apart from hydrogen, most atoms in your body, such as the carbon in your cells and the iron in your blood, were made inside stars long ago.

h: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
t: Astronomers worked this out by studying the faint glow left over from the Big Bang and how fast galaxies are moving apart.

h: Shooting stars aren't stars at all.
t: They're streaks of light made by bits of space dust, many no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up as they zip into Earth's atmosphere.

h: A comet's tail points away from the Sun.
t: Sunlight and the solar wind push the comet's gas and dust outward, so the tail can even lead the way as a comet heads back out into space.

h: Halley's Comet comes back about every 76 years.
t: Its last visit was in 1986, and it's expected to return to the inner solar system in 2061.

h: The asteroid belt is mostly empty space.
t: Asteroids are usually so far apart that spacecraft traveling through the belt haven't needed to dodge them.

h: Pluto has a giant heart.
t: In 2015, the New Horizons spacecraft photographed a huge, bright, heart-shaped region on Pluto, and part of it is a vast plain of frozen nitrogen.

h: Astronauts can grow up to about 3% taller in space.
t: Without gravity squashing them, the cushiony discs in the spine spread out. Astronauts return to their normal height after they come back to Earth.

h: Flames burn in round balls in space.
t: On Earth, hot air rises and stretches a candle flame into a teardrop. In orbit, hot air doesn't rise, so flames form spheres that often glow blue.

h: Space station crews see about 16 sunrises every day.
t: The International Space Station circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes, racing from daylight to darkness and back again.

h: Space is silent.
t: Sound needs air or another material to travel through, and space is almost completely empty, so explosions out there make no noise.

h: The first animals launched into space and brought back alive were fruit flies.
t: In 1947, scientists sent them up on a rocket to study how space radiation might affect living things.

h: Two spacecraft carry a golden record about life on Earth.
t: The Voyager probes, launched in 1977, each carry a gold-plated disc with music, natural sounds and greetings in dozens of languages.

h: Babies have more bones than adults.
t: A newborn starts with nearly 300 bones and cartilage pieces. Many of them fuse together while a child grows, leaving a typical adult with 206.

h: Your smallest bone is about the size of a grain of rice.
t: The stirrup bone, or stapes, sits deep inside your ear and helps pass sound vibrations along to your inner ear.

h: Your hands and feet hold more than half of your bones.
t: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26, which is what makes fingers and toes so flexible.

h: Your thigh bone is your longest and strongest bone.
t: The femur runs from your hip to your knee and supports much of your weight when you stand, walk and jump.

h: One bone in your body isn't connected to any other bone.
t: The horseshoe-shaped hyoid bone in your neck is held in place by muscles and ligaments, and it helps you swallow and speak.

h: Muscles can only pull, never push.
t: That's why they work in teams. When your biceps tightens to bend your arm, your triceps tightens to straighten it again.

h: Your biggest muscle is the one you sit on.
t: The gluteus maximus helps you stand up, climb stairs and keep your body upright.

h: You're a little taller in the morning.
t: During the day, the soft discs between your spine bones get slightly squashed. They spread out again while you sleep, so you wake up around a centimeter taller.

h: Your brain is an energy hog.
t: It makes up only about 2% of your body weight but uses roughly 20% of your body's energy.

h: Your brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.
t: These cells, called neurons, constantly send signals to each other through trillions of connections.

h: The brain itself can't feel pain.
t: It has no pain sensors of its own. Headaches come from the nerves, muscles and blood vessels around the brain, not from the brain tissue.

h: Some nerve signals travel faster than a high-speed train.
t: The fastest signals zip along at about 120 meters per second, which is more than 400 km/h.

h: You can't tickle yourself.
t: Your brain predicts exactly how your own fingers will move, so it turns down the surprise that makes tickling feel ticklish.

h: Your brain is wrinkly for a good reason.
t: All those folds pack a large thinking surface into a small space, the way crumpling a sheet of paper lets it fit into your fist.

h: Yawns are contagious.
t: Seeing, hearing or even reading about someone yawning can make you yawn too. Scientists are still studying exactly why.

h: Brain freeze starts in the roof of your mouth.
t: When something icy touches your palate, blood vessels there quickly change size, and nerves send a signal that your brain feels as a sudden ache in your forehead.

h: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
t: That adds up to billions of beats over a lifetime, all without you ever having to think about it.

h: Your heart is roughly the size of your fist.
t: It sits in the middle of your chest, tilted slightly to the left.

h: Your heart has its own built-in spark plug.
t: A small cluster of special cells called the sinoatrial node sends out tiny electrical signals that set the rhythm of every heartbeat.

h: The "lub-dub" sound is your heart's doors closing.
t: Each beat's two sounds come from valves inside the heart snapping shut to keep blood flowing in the right direction.

h: Red blood cells don't have a nucleus.
t: Skipping the nucleus leaves more room to carry oxygen. Each red blood cell lasts about four months before it's replaced.

h: Your blood makes a full trip around your body in about a minute.
t: When you're resting, your heart pumps roughly your entire blood supply every minute or so.

h: Your left lung is smaller than your right.
t: The left lung has two sections instead of three, which leaves room for your heart.

h: Your lungs are packed with hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs.
t: These sacs, called alveoli, are where oxygen passes into your blood. Spread out flat, their surface would cover the floor of a small apartment.

h: The "hic" in a hiccup is your vocal cords snapping shut.
t: A hiccup begins with a sudden twitch of the diaphragm, the muscle under your lungs, which makes you gulp air just as your vocal cords close.

h: Much of what you call taste is really smell.
t: Your tongue senses only a few basic tastes, such as sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury. Your nose adds the rest, which is why food seems bland when you have a stuffy nose.

h: Your nose has about 400 kinds of smell detectors.
t: Different smells switch on different combinations of these receptors, letting you tell apart a huge variety of scents.

h: Your taste buds are constantly being replaced.
t: Taste cells only last about one to two weeks before new ones take their place.

h: Your eyes see the world upside down.
t: The lens in each eye flips the image it projects onto the back of your eye, and your brain turns it right side up.

h: Each eye has a blind spot.
t: There are no light sensors where the optic nerve leaves the eye, but your brain cleverly fills in the gap, so you never notice.

h: The clear front of your eye gets oxygen straight from the air.
t: The cornea has no blood vessels, which helps keep it perfectly see-through.

h: Your inner ears help you balance.
t: Tiny loops filled with fluid sense when your head moves. After you spin, the fluid keeps swirling for a moment, which is why the room seems to keep spinning.

h: Your smallest muscle is inside your ear.
t: The stapedius muscle is just a millimeter or two long, and it helps steady your tiniest bone when sounds get loud.

h: You blink more than 10,000 times a day.
t: Each blink spreads a fresh layer of tears across your eyes to keep them clean and moist.

h: Your skin is your largest organ.
t: It protects you from germs, helps control your temperature and lets you feel touch, heat and cold.

h: Your outer skin is always being renewed.
t: You shed tiny flakes of skin all day long, and the top layer is replaced about every month.

h: Your hair and nails are made of the same stuff as a rhino's horn.
t: They're all built from a tough protein called keratin, which is also found in hooves, claws and feathers.

h: Fingernails grow faster than toenails.
t: Nobody knows the full reason, but it may be linked to fingers being more active and having better blood flow.

h: Goosebumps are a leftover from furrier ancestors.
t: Tiny muscles pull your hairs upright when you're cold or scared. On a furry animal, that fluffs up the coat for warmth or to look bigger.

h: Your fingerprints formed before you were born.
t: They take shape in the first few months of growth before birth, and even identical twins have different fingerprints.

h: Wrinkly bath fingers are controlled by your nerves.
t: Your fingertips wrinkle in water because blood vessels under the skin narrow. Some scientists think the wrinkles may help you grip wet objects.

h: The hair on your head grows about a centimeter a month.
t: Each strand grows from its own follicle, and a scalp has roughly 100,000 of them.

h: Your stomach lining replaces itself every few days.
t: Your stomach makes strong acid to break down food, so its inner surface is constantly renewed and coated in protective mucus.

h: A growling stomach doesn't always mean you're hungry.
t: The rumbling comes from muscles squeezing food, liquid and gas through your gut, and it can happen at any time. It's just louder when your stomach is empty.

h: The DNA in one cell would stretch about two meters.
t: Your body tightly coils that long thread so it fits inside a nucleus far too small to see without a microscope.

h: You are made of tens of trillions of cells.
t: They come in hundreds of types, from long, thin nerve cells to round, flexible red blood cells.

h: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in your body.
t: It's even harder than bone, which helps your teeth crush and grind food for many years.

h: Humans are the only living animals with true chins.
t: Scientists still debate why our jaws grew this way, since even our closest animal relatives don't have them.

h: Your body gives off about as much heat as a light bulb.
t: At rest, an adult makes roughly 80 to 100 watts of heat, which is why a room full of people warms up quickly.

h: Your liver can regrow.
t: If part of a healthy liver is removed, the rest can grow back to close to its original size in a matter of weeks.

h: The ocean covers about 71% of Earth's surface.
t: Seen from space, our planet looks mostly blue, which is why it's often called the Blue Planet.

h: About 97% of Earth's water is in the ocean.
t: Only a small share is fresh water, and much of that is locked away in ice and underground.

h: There is really just one world ocean.
t: The Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern Oceans are all connected, so water can flow between them.

h: The Pacific is the biggest ocean.
t: It's so large that all the land on Earth could fit inside it with room to spare.

h: The average depth of the ocean is about 3,700 meters.
t: That's deeper than many mountain peaks are tall.

h: Most of the ocean has never been explored by people.
t: Large areas of the deep sea have never been visited or seen up close, and our maps of the seafloor are far less detailed than our maps of the Moon.

h: The ocean is blue because water soaks up red light.
t: Water absorbs the red, orange and yellow parts of sunlight more than the blue, so blue light is what bounces back to our eyes.

h: The deepest known spot is about 11 kilometers down.
t: It's called the Challenger Deep, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean.

h: Mount Everest would disappear in the Mariana Trench.
t: If you dropped the world's highest mountain into the deepest point, its peak would still be more than two kilometers underwater.

h: The pressure at the bottom of the deepest trench is enormous.
t: It's more than 1,000 times the air pressure we feel at sea level, which is why only specially built vehicles can survive a trip down there.

h: Sunlight fades out quickly underwater.
t: Below about 200 meters, there isn't enough light for plants or algae to grow, and below about 1,000 meters it is completely dark.

h: Seawater can be hotter than boiling without bubbling.
t: Hydrothermal vents on the seafloor shoot out water above 350 °C, but the crushing pressure stops it from boiling.

h: Whole communities live around those vents in total darkness.
t: Instead of relying on sunlight, the base of their food chain is bacteria that make energy from chemicals pouring out of the vents.

h: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived.
t: It's bigger than any dinosaur, and one preserved blue whale heart weighed about 180 kilograms, as much as two or three adults.

h: Many deep-sea creatures can make their own light.
t: This glow, called bioluminescence, helps them find food, attract mates, confuse predators and signal to each other.

h: Ocean algae make a huge share of the oxygen we breathe.
t: Tiny drifting plant-like life called phytoplankton produce an estimated half of the oxygen made on Earth.

h: Sea stars don't have blood.
t: Instead, they pump seawater through a network of canals to move their hundreds of tiny tube feet.

h: Jellyfish have no brain, heart or bones.
t: They are mostly water, yet they've drifted through the oceans for hundreds of millions of years.

h: Sea turtles find their way back to the beaches where they hatched.
t: Scientists believe they navigate partly by sensing Earth's magnetic field.

h: Some kelp can grow more than half a meter in a single day.
t: Giant kelp forms underwater forests that shelter fish, seals and sea otters.

h: Parrotfish help make sandy beaches.
t: They bite off chunks of coral to eat the algae on it, and grind the hard bits into fine sand that comes out the other end.

h: Some parrotfish sleep in a bubble of slime.
t: At night they wrap themselves in a mucus cocoon that seems to help protect them from tiny parasites while they rest.

h: Sharks have been around longer than trees.
t: Sharks first appeared more than 400 million years ago, while the earliest trees showed up later.

h: Greenland sharks may live for centuries.
t: A study of their eyes suggested some of these slow-moving sharks could be more than 250 years old, making them the longest-living vertebrates known.

h: Octopuses can taste with their arms.
t: Their suckers are lined with sensors that let them taste and feel whatever they touch.

h: Clownfish live safely among stinging anemones.
t: A special layer of slime on their skin protects them from the anemone's stings, and in return they help chase away fish that would nibble on the anemone.

h: The Moon is the main cause of the tides.
t: The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans, making the sea level rise and fall, usually twice a day along most coasts.

h: The Bay of Fundy has some of the highest tides on Earth.
t: In this bay between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in Canada, the water can rise and fall by about 16 meters.

h: The Gulf Stream moves more water than all the world's rivers combined.
t: This powerful current carries warm tropical water up along the east coast of North America and across the Atlantic toward Europe.

h: Wind makes most ocean waves.
t: As wind blows across the water, it passes along energy that can travel thousands of kilometers before the waves reach a shore.

h: Tsunami waves can travel as fast as a jet plane.
t: In the deep ocean, these waves race along at hundreds of kilometers an hour, but they only grow tall as they reach shallow water.

h: There's a giant waterfall under the ocean.
t: Between Greenland and Iceland, cold, heavy water spills down a slope on the seafloor called the Denmark Strait cataract, dropping about 3.5 kilometers.

h: The ocean has a slow global "conveyor belt."
t: Cold, salty water sinks near the poles and drifts along the bottom of the sea, and scientists estimate a single drop can take around a thousand years to complete the loop.

h: Rubber ducks helped scientists study currents.
t: In 1992, thousands of bath toys fell off a cargo ship in the Pacific, and people tracking where they washed up learned more about how ocean currents flow.

h: Most of the ocean's salt came from rocks on land.
t: Rain slowly wears away rocks, and rivers carry tiny amounts of dissolved minerals out to sea, where they build up over time.

h: If you dried up the ocean, the salt could bury the land.
t: Spread evenly over Earth's land, the ocean's salt would make a layer more than 150 meters thick.

h: Salt water freezes at a colder temperature than fresh water.
t: Typical seawater freezes at about −2 °C instead of 0 °C.

h: Sea ice is mostly fresh.
t: When ocean water freezes, most of the salt gets pushed out of the ice and left behind in the water below.

h: Salty water helps you float.
t: Salt makes water denser, so it pushes up harder on you, which is why it's easier to float in the sea than in a swimming pool.

h: There are lakes and rivers on the ocean floor.
t: In some places, extra-salty water collects in dips on the seafloor and forms "brine pools" with their own shorelines.

h: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure built by living things.
t: Stretching more than 2,000 kilometers along Australia's coast, it's made by countless tiny coral animals.

h: Coral is an animal, not a plant.
t: Each coral is made of tiny creatures called polyps, and many of them get food from tiny algae living inside their bodies.

h: The longest mountain range on Earth is underwater.
t: The mid-ocean ridge winds around the globe for about 65,000 kilometers, mostly hidden beneath the sea.

h: Mauna Kea is taller than Everest if you measure from its base.
t: This Hawaiian volcano starts far down on the seafloor and rises more than 10,000 meters to its peak.

h: Most of Earth's volcanic eruptions happen underwater.
t: Much of this activity takes place along the mid-ocean ridges, deep beneath the waves, where new seafloor is constantly forming.

h: Bamboo is a giant grass.
t: It's one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth, and some species can shoot up by close to a meter in a single day.

h: Young sunflowers follow the Sun.
t: Growing sunflowers turn east to west through the day and swing back at night. Once they're fully grown, most settle facing east, which helps them warm up in the morning and attract more bees.

h: One of the biggest living things is a forest that's really one tree.
t: A grove of quaking aspens in Utah, nicknamed Pando, has tens of thousands of trunks that all sprout from the same connected root system. Genetically, it's a single plant.

h: Venus flytraps can count.
t: A trap usually snaps shut only when two of its trigger hairs are touched within about 20 seconds, so a falling raindrop won't fool it. In the wild, these plants grow only in a small area of North and South Carolina.

h: A dandelion is a bouquet in disguise.
t: What looks like one yellow flower is really a tightly packed head of many tiny flowers, and each one can turn into a single fluffy seed.

h: Some trees are older than the pyramids of Egypt.
t: Some bristlecone pines growing high in the mountains of the western United States are close to 5,000 years old, so they had already sprouted when the Great Pyramid was being built.

h: Giant sequoias can handle fire.
t: Their spongy bark can be thicker than a hand is long, which shields them from flames, and the heat from a forest fire helps their cones open and release seeds.

h: Fireflies make light without getting hot.
t: Their glow comes from a chemical reaction inside their bodies that gives off very little heat, which is why it's sometimes called "cold light."

h: Tardigrades are incredibly tough.
t: These tiny eight-legged animals, nicknamed water bears, can survive drying out, deep freezing and even a trip outside a spacecraft in the vacuum of space.

h: Axolotls can regrow body parts.
t: These smiling salamanders from Mexico can regrow lost legs, parts of their spinal cord and even pieces of their heart.

h: Peacock feathers aren't really green and blue.
t: Their shimmering colors come from microscopic structures that bend and reflect light, not from colored pigment. That's why the colors shift as the bird moves.

h: A fluffy cloud can hold hundreds of metric tons of water.
t: The water is spread out in countless tiny droplets floating in rising air, so the cloud stays up even though all that water together is incredibly heavy.

h: Snowflakes have six sides for a reason.
t: The way water molecules link together as they freeze creates a six-sided pattern, so snowflakes usually grow six arms or six corners.

h: "Alphabet" comes from the first two Greek letters.
t: Alpha and beta were joined together to name the whole set of letters.

h: The dot over a lowercase i has a name.
t: It's called a tittle. The dot on a j is a tittle too.

h: "Robot" first appeared in a play.
t: Czech writer Karel Čapek introduced it in his 1920 play R.U.R., using a word related to the Czech "robota," meaning forced labor. He credited his brother Josef with suggesting it.

h: One famous sentence uses every letter of the alphabet.
t: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" is a pangram, and typists have used it for generations to test keyboards and typefaces.

h: "Goodbye" is a shortened blessing.
t: It started out centuries ago as "God be with ye" and was squeezed down over time.

h: The & symbol is a squashed Latin word.
t: The ampersand began as a fancy way of writing "et," Latin for "and." Its name comes from schoolchildren reciting "and per se and" at the end of the alphabet.

h: "Bookkeeper" has three double letters in a row.
t: Look closely: oo, kk, ee.

h: "Typewriter" can be typed using only the top row of letters.
t: On a standard keyboard, every letter in the word sits on the top row.

h: "Rhythm" has no a, e, i, o or u.
t: The letter y does the work of a vowel in words like rhythm, gym and myth.

h: "Nice" used to be an insult.
t: The word comes from a Latin word meaning "not knowing," and in medieval English it meant foolish or silly. Its meaning shifted many times before it became a compliment.

h: "Quarantine" means forty.
t: It comes from the Italian for "forty days," the length of time some ships arriving in Venice had to wait before passengers could come ashore.

h: "Emoji" has nothing to do with "emotion."
t: The word is Japanese, combining "e," meaning picture, and "moji," meaning written character.

h: "OK" began as a joke.
t: In 1839, a Boston newspaper used "o.k." as a playful abbreviation of "oll korrect," a deliberate misspelling of "all correct." The joke caught on and spread around the world.

h: Rainbows are actually circles.
t: From the ground, the horizon cuts off the bottom half, so we see an arch. From an airplane or a high mountain, you can sometimes spot a full ring.

h: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
t: A lightning bolt can heat the air around it to roughly five times the temperature of the Sun's surface. The air expands so suddenly that it makes the boom we call thunder.

h: You can tell how far away a storm is.
t: Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder. Every three seconds means the lightning is about one kilometer away.

h: Raindrops aren't shaped like teardrops.
t: Small raindrops are round, and bigger ones get flattened on the bottom by the air rushing past, so they look more like hamburger buns.

h: The sky is blue because air scatters blue light.
t: Sunlight contains every color, but tiny gas molecules in the air scatter blue light much more than red. At sunset, light travels through so much air that most of the blue is scattered away, leaving oranges and reds.

h: Ice floats because water is unusual.
t: Most substances shrink as they freeze, but water expands. That makes ice lighter than the water around it, so lakes freeze from the top down and fish can survive the winter underneath.

h: Diamonds and pencil marks are made of the same thing.
t: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. The only difference is how the carbon atoms are arranged.

h: Only two elements are liquid at room temperature.
t: They're mercury, a metal, and bromine, a reddish-brown liquid. Every other element is a solid or a gas at a comfortable room temperature.

h: The air you breathe is mostly not oxygen.
t: About 78 percent of air is nitrogen, and only about 21 percent is oxygen.

h: Gold can be hammered incredibly thin.
t: A single gram of gold can be beaten into a sheet about a meter on each side, so thin that light can shine through it.

h: Sound travels more than four times faster in water than in air.
t: Sound needs something to travel through, so in the near-empty vacuum of space, there's no sound at all.

h: Helium doesn't change your vocal cords.
t: It makes your voice sound squeaky because sound travels faster through helium than through air, which changes how your voice resonates in your throat and mouth.

h: Bananas are very slightly radioactive.
t: They contain potassium, and a tiny fraction of natural potassium is radioactive. The amount is far too small to do any harm.

h: The tiny pocket in your jeans was made for a watch.
t: Long before wristwatches were common, workers carried pocket watches, and that little pocket kept them safe.

h: The plastic tip on a shoelace is called an aglet.
t: It keeps the end from fraying and makes it easy to thread the lace through the holes.

h: Many pen caps have a hole for safety.
t: The small hole lets air pass through if a cap is ever accidentally swallowed, which lowers the risk of choking.

h: Airplane windows have a tiny hole on purpose.
t: The little hole in the middle pane balances the air pressure between the layers, so the outer pane takes the strain. It also helps stop the window from fogging up.

h: The QWERTY keyboard was designed for typewriters.
t: Its layout was developed in the 1870s for early mechanical typewriters, and it has stuck around ever since.

h: Bumpy packing wrap was first meant to be wallpaper.
t: In 1957, two engineers sealed two shower curtains together trying to create textured wallpaper. It didn't catch on as decoration, but it turned out to be perfect for protecting packages.

h: The first product ever scanned with a barcode was chewing gum.
t: In 1974, a pack of gum became the first item rung up with a barcode scanner at a supermarket checkout in Ohio.

h: The first traffic signal was put up before cars existed.
t: It was installed outside the Houses of Parliament in London in 1868 to direct horse-drawn carriages, and a police officer had to operate it by hand.

h: Pencil "lead" has never been made of lead.
t: It's a mix of graphite and clay. The name stuck because people long ago mistook graphite for a kind of lead.

h: The F and J keys have little bumps for a reason.
t: They let touch typists find the home row with their fingers without looking down at the keyboard.

h: Many clocks write four as IIII.
t: Clock faces with Roman numerals often show four as IIII instead of IV. It's a long tradition, and many people think it makes the dial look more balanced.

h: Tin cans were invented decades before the can opener.
t: Food was being sealed in metal cans in the early 1800s, but practical can openers didn't appear until the 1850s. Before that, people opened cans with a hammer and chisel.

h: Australia is wider than the Moon.
t: The Moon is about 3,475 kilometers across, while mainland Australia stretches roughly 4,000 kilometers from east to west.

h: Africa is in all four hemispheres.
t: Both the equator and the prime meridian cross it, so parts of Africa lie in the northern, southern, eastern and western hemispheres. The two lines meet in the ocean just off its west coast.

h: Measured from its base, Mauna Kea is taller than Mount Everest.
t: Most of this Hawaiian volcano is hidden underwater. From the sea floor to its summit, it rises more than 10,000 meters.

h: Everest's peak isn't the farthest point from Earth's center.
t: Earth bulges at the equator because it spins, so the summit of Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador near the equator, sticks out farther into space.

h: Istanbul sits on two continents.
t: The city is split by a narrow waterway called the Bosphorus, with one side in Europe and the other in Asia.

h: Three countries are completely surrounded by just one other country.
t: Lesotho sits entirely inside South Africa, while Vatican City and San Marino are both surrounded by Italy.

h: Alaska is the most northern, western and eastern US state.
t: Its Aleutian Islands stretch so far west that a few of them cross into the Eastern Hemisphere.

h: The largest desert on Earth is freezing cold.
t: A desert is defined by how little precipitation it gets, not by heat, and Antarctica gets so little that it counts as the biggest desert of all.

h: A town called Boring is partnered with a village called Dull.
t: Boring in Oregon and Dull in Scotland teamed up in 2012 as a fun way to celebrate their names.

h: Four US states meet at a single point.
t: At the Four Corners, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah touch, so you can stand in all four at once.

h: The Panama Canal's Pacific end is east of its Atlantic end.
t: Because of the way Panama curves, ships crossing from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travel toward the southeast.

h: Nepal's flag isn't a rectangle.
t: It's made of two stacked triangles, a shape unlike any other national flag.

h: September means "seventh month."
t: The early Roman calendar began in March, so September, October, November and December were months seven to ten. July and August were later renamed to honor Julius Caesar and Augustus.

h: The Great Pyramid held a height record for about 3,800 years.
t: It was the tallest structure built by humans until a cathedral spire in England rose higher in the 1300s.

h: The ancient Olympic Games began over 2,700 years ago.
t: The first recorded games took place in Greece in 776 BC. The modern Olympics started in Athens in 1896.

h: The Leaning Tower of Pisa started tilting while it was being built.
t: Construction began in 1173, and the soft ground underneath began to sink after only a few levels were finished.

h: Big Ben is the name of a bell.
t: The famous clock tower in London is officially called the Elizabeth Tower. Big Ben is the huge bell inside it.

h: The first Ferris wheel was built to outshine the Eiffel Tower.
t: Engineer George Ferris designed it for the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago, and its cars could carry dozens of riders each.

h: Machu Picchu's walls were built without mortar.
t: Inca builders shaped many of the stones so precisely that they fit snugly together, with no cement holding them in place.

h: Farmers digging a well found a clay army.
t: In 1974, farmers in China uncovered the Terracotta Army, thousands of life-size clay figures made more than 2,000 years ago, each finished with its own details such as hairstyles and facial features.

h: Some of Stonehenge's stones traveled from Wales.
t: Its smaller bluestones came from hills about 240 kilometers away, and researchers are still studying exactly how people moved them.

h: The teddy bear is named after a president.
t: After a 1902 newspaper cartoon showed President Theodore Roosevelt refusing to harm a bear, a shop owner began selling stuffed toy bears named after "Teddy."

h: The pyramid builders lived in their own town.
t: Archaeologists have found the remains of a workers' village near the Giza pyramids, complete with bakeries and sleeping quarters, showing the builders were organized, well-fed crews.

h: An 11-year-old named Pluto.
t: In 1930, Venetia Burney, a schoolgirl in England, suggested the name for the newly discovered world, and astronomers chose it.
